text: It seems like we saw an unprompted attack by Iran this morning.
And when I say unprompted, I just mean that over the past few days,
we have seen a sense of calmness, really, in the Middle East
that follows the United States without explanation on Friday,
halting attacks against Iran after 13 consecutive nights of hitting targets within Iran.
So what we saw overnight is Iran attacking military bases, U.S. military bases.
Those were all intercepted, according to the United States Central Command.
But still, it looks like Iran had done a preemptive strike of some sorts in the early hours of the morning.
We also saw Jordan reporting that five missiles by Iran were launched at its territories.
And so we're seeing a slight tick up in the escalations in the Middle East, again, as I mentioned,
after days of calmness that were in the environment here.
And so what we're looking at is the price of crude, as you've mentioned in your intro,
at about $87 on the barrel.
It was sticking up 4%.
It still is, as a matter of fact, 4% higher because of these escalations that we're seeing in the region.
Obviously, Anna, at the heart of all of this, remains the Strait of Hormuz.
And the still paralyzed movement there.
But we're not just looking at one waterway now.
We're looking at two waterways because Ras al-Mandeb, Bab al-Mandeb, which is in the Red Sea,
and which Saudi Arabia has been resorting to as an ulterior pathway to get its crude shipments across,
is now also at risk because we're seeing the Yemen Houthis, which are backed by Iran,
also attacking it and going for these stit-fratat strikes there.
So across the board, risk on in the region, we continue to obviously monitor what the United States wakes up to
and what President Trump decides to do.
And so where do we see it all going if the fighting escalates further?
Yeah, it's a good question, Lizzie.
I mean, we are anticipating the potential of further escalation in the region.
Those stit-fratat strikes have been happening.
And again, just remember that the halting of the attacks by the United States on Friday
came without explanation from the U.S. side.
We understand from multiple media reports that that could have been due to possibly diminishing munition power by the United States.
President Trump obviously came out and refuted that, saying that the United States had more than enough munition,
that he would love for the United States to have more, but that it has the power to continue fighting Iran.
Iran, on the other side, has the ability, Lizzie, to manufacture those drones for quite cheap.
And so it has the ability to keep hitting countries in the region.
And that is what it has shown.
But meanwhile, what we're monitoring very closely and what is impacting that price of brand and crude generally
is those talks between Oman and Iran to open a so-called middle passageway in the Strait of Hormuz,
a pathway that has not been used throughout the course of this war
because Iran has been asking ships to continue to stick to the northern side of the Strait of Hormuz, close to its borders.
So if that were to happen, that potentially gives ships and tankers
that are trying to make their way through the Strait of Hormuz a little bit more ability
to start making their shipments or having their shipments come across the waterway.
Those conversations are not finalized.
We're reporting that they're still going on.
And we'll continue to monitor whether they actually lead to some kind of conclusion
where ships can finally start moving a little bit more freely in the Strait of Hormuz.
